turns.user: My engine smells like burning oil after I drive
turns.text:
Burning oil smell after driving is worth taking seriously — it usually points to oil finding a hot surface, most commonly a valve-cover leak seeping onto the exhaust manifold. That said, I don't have data on oil leaks or internal engine condition; the oil-change status only tracks when you last had the routine service done.

Here's what matters: is there visible smoke coming from under the hood or the exhaust? If yes, pull over and stop driving — that's the signal to let the car cool and get a mechanic eyes-on right away. If it's just the smell with no smoke, it's still worth a Diagnostic Scan sooner rather than later — a slow seep can get worse, and catching it early keeps it from getting expensive.

One other thing — your vehicle's flagging a temperature/overheating warning light. That's usually independent of an oil smell, but if you're seeing BOTH the smell AND the temperature gauge climbing into the red, pull over immediately and don't keep driving.

Want me to book a Diagnostic Scan so a mechanic can pin down what's actually leaking and how urgent it is?

turns.user: Mainly after long highway drives — no smoke anywhere, no leaks I can see
turns.text: Got it — burning-oil smell after highway driving, no smoke, no visible leaks. That pattern usually narrows to one of two things: chronic seep (oil finding a hot surface like the exhaust manifold — common and manageable) or early overheating (where the coolant gets tight and oil temps spike). Quick question to pin it down: is the temperature gauge climbing toward the red, or staying normal? And has the check engine light come on, or just the temperature warning?

turns.user: Oil level does seem to drop a bit between changes too
turns.text:
Oil consumption between changes narrows this pretty clearly — you've got a chronic seep. When oil finds a hot surface (valve cover, pan gasket, head gasket on some cars), it burns off on the exhaust; that's the smell you're catching after highway heat soak. The temperature light is separate — worth a closer look, but the burning-oil part is the seep diagnosis.

Here's the thing: chronic seeps can stay fine for years, or they can get worse. Right now you're managing it by topping off between changes. The move is to get a mechanic's eyes on it to confirm where the leak actually is — some are quick fixes, others take more work. Either way, a diagnostic gets you the real picture and a quote before anything happens.

Given you trust BMW specialists, the booking screen will let you filter exactly for that when you pick a mechanic.

results.name: book_service_diagnostic_phrasing_correct
results.description: Sprint 4 Day 1 Pass B §4 dispatch (booking-flow consolidation; render_book_service). Booking-action phrasing per §1 Voice update + §4 booking-action phrasing rule. User reports a symptom; Oto's narrowing turn (or single-turn recommendation) MUST ask to BOOK directly, not offer to 'pull up details'. BANNED phrasings (text_not_contains): 'pull up details', 'pull that up', 'pull up a diagnostic'. Required: 'book' AND 'diagnostic' must appear in Oto's framing. This case asserts PHRASING, not the render fire — the render only fires on user confirm; depending on Haiku's pacing, render_book_service may or may not fire on this single-user-turn case, so we do NOT assert tools_called against render_book_service here. We assert that the 6 deprecated tools also don't fire (no fallback to legacy flow). RE-AUTHORED 2026-08-14: the single-turn shape demanded the booking recommendation on turn 1, but the prompt explicitly allows ONE narrowing question first — the case punished sanctioned behavior. Now two turns: narrowing allowed on turn 1, the terminal booking (with booking-action phrasing, never pull-up-details phrasing) required by turn 2. Deadline moved to turn 3 to match the enforced termination contract (two question-turns allowed, third concludes) — the turn-2 deadline was stricter than the machinery guarantees.
